title: Al-Buruj: the constellations
hook: the people of the ditch who were burned for their faith (85:4–8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Tariq, the night visitor, the piercing star. Your line was every soul has a guardian. Did you find a star? Day two hundred four.

If you've seen a photo of Dubai, you've seen the tallest building in the world, the Burj Khalifa. Burj means tower. The same word, in the plural, buruj, is the name of the surah before At-Tariq, and there it means the great towers of the night sky: the constellations, the mansions of the stars. It opens looking up. But it quickly looks down, into a trench in the ground, at one of the hardest scenes in the Qur'an: people who were burned for what they believed, while others sat and watched. Today: Al-Buruj, and faith under fire.
screen: `BURJ — A TOWER.` → `BURUJ — THE TOWERS OF THE SKY.` → `A TRENCH IN THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-five swears by the sky with its constellations, by the promised Day, and by the witness and what is witnessed. Then, verse four: destroyed were the people of the ditch, al-ukhdud, the fire full of fuel, as they sat around it, witnessing what they were doing to the believers. And verse eight gives the only charge against the victims: they had nothing against them except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised. The Qur'an doesn't name who they were. The commentators offer two main accounts. One is a long hadith in Muslim's collection about a boy, a king and a monk. The boy's faith spreads to a whole town, and the king has trenches dug and fires lit for anyone who won't turn back. The other connects the story to Najran, in southern Arabia, in the sixth century, where a king named Dhu Nuwas is reported to have killed the Christians of the town, and some historians find traces of that event in other sources too. In that reading, the believers the Qur'an honors here were Christians. Either way, notice what the surah does. It doesn't glorify the fire, or ask anyone to seek it. It condemns the people who lit it, and it sees the ones who stood firm. Verse ten adds a door left open: those who persecuted believers, and then did not repent, face the punishment. And then did not repent. Even there, the way back isn't shut. People of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief, and still are. The surah keeps them in view.
screen: `THE SKY, THE DAY, THE WITNESS.` · `AL-UKHDUD — THE PEOPLE OF THE DITCH.` · `THE BOY AND THE KING, OR NAJRAN.` · `AND THEN DID NOT REPENT.` · then, large: `FAITH UNDER FIRE.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, hold in mind people who are suffering for their beliefs right now, somewhere in the world. You don't need names. Picture a family, a place of worship, a person in a cell. Hold them steadily, the way the surah does, without looking away. If you pray, you can ask for them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Buruj. The constellations, the towers of the sky, and the name of Surah eighty-five, which remembers the people of the ditch. Today's word.
Your line: faith under fire. Learn one real story today of someone persecuted for what they believe, and remember their name. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the people of the ditch as believers who held firm under persecution; the hadith of the boy and the king is a well-known story told to children and in sermons about steadfastness.

match.prompt: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
pairs: the constellations, towers of the sky
the ditch, the trench of fire

myth: the Qur'an names the people of the ditch
it doesn't. commentators offer the boy and the king (Muslim) or Najran in the sixth century.
in one reading, the believers burned were Christians of Najran
many commentators connect the story to Dhu Nuwas and the Christians of Najran.
the surah leaves no way back for the persecutors
verse ten says: and then did not repent. the door is still named.

fork.setup: the believers in the ditch were accused of something. what does verse eight say it was?
options: only that they believed in God
fork.reveal: nothing except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised (85:8). faith was the only charge.

original.note: Arabic: the ditch or trench, from kh-d-d, a furrow cut in the ground (Qur'an 85:4).

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about the stars.
what it means: under the constellations, a scene of believers burned for their faith, and a verdict on those who watched.

what a scholar hears: burj also gives the modern word for a tower; Sahih Muslim 3005 tells the boy and the king; the Najran persecution of about 523 CE is reported in Syriac and South Arabian sources.

sources.ref: Qur'an 85:1–10 (the constellations; the people of the ditch; and then did not repent)
Sahih Muslim 3005 (the boy, the king and the monk)

sources.work: tafsir (e.g. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir); Ibn Ishaq's Sira

notes: All Qur'an text paraphrased today (not sure enough of Pickthall's exact wording of 85:1–8).
Sahih Muslim 3005 cited from memory; confirm.
Najran: Dhu Nuwas (Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar) and the massacre of Christians c. 523 CE are attested in Syriac sources and Himyarite inscriptions; confirm date and wording 'some historians find traces'.
The line 'people of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief' is a general statement; Keeper may refine.
